title: Avoiding unintended mutations through shared references / Counting values with collections.Counter

steps.title: Avoiding unintended mutations through shared references

blocks.text: Different names can refer to one object: assignment is not a copy. Mutating a shared list or dictionary can be visible through another name and to a caller.
items.copy() or items[:] makes a shallow list copy: top-level changes are independent, but references to existing elements remain. A nested mutable element can still be shared.

blocks.title: Separate outer lists, shared inner list
blocks.alt_text: original and alias point to one outer list. copied points to another outer list. Both outer lists reference the same existing inner list. An append through alias changes the shared outer list; a nested update through copied changes the shared inner list.

blocks.text: alias and original share an outer list, so appending through alias affects original. copied has a separate outer list, so that append does not affect its top level. Updating an existing inner element through copied is visible through original because the inner list is shared. original[:] also makes a shallow copy.

blocks.code:
original = [[3, 2]]
alias = original
copied = original.copy()
alias.append([5])
copied[0][0] = 9
print(original)
print(copied)

public.prompt:
Before repair, what is original after this helper call?
```python
def append_copy(items):
    copied = items
    copied.append([5])
    return copied

original = [[3, 2]]
changed = append_copy(original)
```

options.text: The caller's list is unaffected because the helper uses the name items.

o2.message: No copy is made: the top-level append changes the caller's list.

o3.message: Changing the name does not copy the object; mutation can remain visible to the caller.

blocks.text: After from collections import Counter, Counter(items) counts occurrences of hashable elements, mapping each element to its count. Use it to summarize repeated stationery labels.
counts.most_common(1) returns a list containing the most frequent element/count pair, or an empty list for an empty counter. Check that the list is nonempty before selecting its first pair.
most_common orders pairs by descending count. Tied counts follow first encounter, not a separate ranking. Compare the repeated-label example with empty input and a tie using the same labels.

blocks.code:
from collections import Counter
counts = Counter(["blue", "red", "blue"])
print(counts)
pairs = counts.most_common(1)
print(pairs)
if pairs:
    label, count = pairs[0]
    print(label, count)

from collections import Counter

pairs = counts.most_common(1)

segments.label: Import Counter and inspect element counts
segments.summary: Import Counter from collections to use it directly. Passing a string counts its characters; passing a list counts repeated values. The examples also supply existing counts through a dictionary and keyword arguments. Displayed results associate each element with its count. Counter has its own type, but its element-to-count structure is a mapping.

bridge.before: Watch how repeated values become element-count entries. The clip loosely distinguishes Counter from dictionaries; Devspace describes its result as a mapping, and counting requires hashable elements.
bridge.after: The clip demonstrates counting, but omits the hashability restriction and most_common. The text supplies these requirements, including empty results, safe first-pair access, descending counts, and first-encounter tie ordering.

solution_files.content:
from collections import Counter
first_label = 'blue'
labels = [first_label, 'red', first_label]
pairs = Counter(labels).most_common(1)

# Repair the pairs assignment; retain the supplied safe reporting block.
if pairs:
    label, count = pairs[0]
    print(label, count)

blocks.title: Inspecting program state with diagnostic printing

blocks.text: alias = original binds another name to the same list; it does not copy. An append through alias is visible through original and can affect a caller sharing that list. Different names do not imply independent objects.

remediation_steps.title: Separate outer list, shared inner element

blocks.text: copied = original.copy() separates the outer list but retains references to existing elements. A nested update through copied can therefore be visible through original. Separate outer lists do not imply separate nested mutable elements.

remediation_steps.title: Copy before changing the top level

blocks.text: Contrast copied = items with copied = items.copy() or copied = items[:]. The first shares the list; either copy form creates a separate outer list, allowing independent top-level changes. Appending to that copied outer list does not append to the caller’s outer list.

remediation_steps.title: A returned list, not a bare pair

blocks.text: Counter counts hashable elements into an element-to-count mapping. most_common(1) returns a list containing the most frequent pair, not the bare pair. An empty counter returns an empty list: check pairs before pairs[0]. Pairs descend by count; ties follow first encounter.

remediation_steps.title: First encounter, not a separate rank

blocks.text: With tied counts among the supplied labels, most_common follows first encounter. It orders by descending count first, not a separate label ranking. Check that the returned list is nonempty before accessing its first pair.
